identity.spiritualSignificanceShort: Bhimashankar is counted among the twelve Jyotirlingas of Shiva and is one of three in Maharashtra. The shrine stands high in the Sahyadri crestline at about 934 m, close to the source of the Bhima river. Its setting inside a notified wildlife sanctuary means a visit is also a walk into protected Western Ghats forest.

governance.establishedEra: Ancient origins; current structure 17th-18th century · Rebuilt during Marathi period

narrative.summaryIntro:
Bhimashankar Temple is one of the twelve Jyotirlingas and is located in the Sahyadri (Western Ghats) mountain range near Pune, Maharashtra. Dedicated to Lord Shiva as Bhimashankar, the temple is situated in a scenic region and is considered one of the most important pilgrimage sites in western India. The temple is named after the Bhima River, which originates nearby and flows through the region.

The temple features traditional Deccan architecture and is surrounded by lush forests and scenic mountain landscapes. The site is a major pilgrimage destination and holds special significance during Maha Shivaratri. The temple's location in the heart of nature makes it a unique combination of spiritual devotion and natural beauty, attracting both pilgrims and nature lovers.
narrative.documentedHistory:
The temple stands in Bhimashankar village in Khed taluka of Pune district, at roughly 19.072°N 73.536°E and an elevation of about 934 m on the Sahyadri crest. The building is carved from black stone and is dated to the 13th century; its architecture is Nagara with affinities to the Hemadpanti idiom common in the Deccan. In the later 18th century Nana Phadnavis built the sabhamandap and designed the shikhara, giving the temple much of its present silhouette. A bell in the complex was donated by Chimaji Appa in 1739, taken after the Maratha defeat of the Portuguese at Vasai fort.

The Bhima river rises near the temple. Several kunds are associated with the site, including Mokshakund, where pilgrims traditionally bathe before entering, Jnyankund, and Sarvatirth; the Kamalaja Mata temple stands nearby.

The temple sits inside the Bhimashankar Wildlife Sanctuary, notified in October 1985 for the conservation of the Indian giant squirrel (locally Shekru), the state animal of Maharashtra. The sanctuary occupies the crestline of the northern Western Ghats across Pune and Thane districts; its major forest types run from western subtropical broad-leaved hill forest to moist deciduous, with small included patches of evergreen forest. A 2017 floristic survey published in the Journal of Threatened Taxa recorded 1,142 angiospermic taxa there in 619 genera and 124 families, of which 217 are Indian endemics and 53 fall within IUCN threat categories.

The Pune district administration's own tourism listing independently records Bhimashankar as one of the twelve Jyotirlingas, describes the temple as an example of 13th-century architecture, and attributes the sabhamandap and shikhara to Nana Phadnavis in the 18th century.
